title: Lesson 14: فِعْل الْأَمْر — Building the Command in Four Steps
summary: The class meets the third type of verb. Where the مَاضِي and the مُضَارِع both convey information, فِعْل الْأَمْر asks for something to be done. The teacher lays out a four-step procedure for deriving the command from the present tense — strip the prefix, attach هَمْزَة الْوَصْل, make the final letter sākin, then let the vowel on the third letter decide the vowel on the hamza — and the class tests it on verb after verb, almost all of them traced to a Qur'ānic command.
key_points: Arabic has three types of verb: الْمَاضِي (past), الْمُضَارِع (present or future), and فِعْل الْأَمْر (the command). The first two give information about what happened or is happening; the command instead asks for an action.
Step one: look at the مُضَارِع form of the verb, and especially at the vowel on its third letter.
Step two: remove the prefix letter and put هَمْزَة الْوَصْل in its place.
Step three: make the final letter مَجْزُوم, that is sākin — اُكْتُبْ, not اُكْتُبُ.

Step four: decide the vowel on the hamza. It is never a fatḥa. If the third letter carries a ḍamma, the hamza takes a ḍamma (يَكْتُبُ gives اُكْتُبْ); if the third letter carries a kasra or a fatḥa, the hamza takes a kasra (يَجْلِسُ gives اِجْلِسْ, يَذْهَبُ gives اِذْهَبْ).

Worked through in class: ذَهَبَ، يَذْهَبُ، اِذْهَبْ; دَخَلَ، يَدْخُلُ، اُدْخُلْ; كَتَبَ، يَكْتُبُ، اُكْتُبْ; جَلَسَ، يَجْلِسُ، اِجْلِسْ; قَرَأَ، يَقْرَأُ، اِقْرَأْ; قَتَلَ، يَقْتُلُ، اُقْتُلْ; نَظَرَ، يَنْظُرُ، اُنْظُرْ; دَفَعَ، يَدْفَعُ، اِدْفَعْ; سَمِعَ، يَسْمَعُ، اِسْمَعْ; غَسَلَ، يَغْسِلُ، اِغْسِلْ; حَفِظَ، يَحْفَظُ، اِحْفَظْ.
These forms address one male. For a group of males a wāw is added — اُقْتُلُوا، اُنْظُرُوا، اُعْبُدُوا — and the other persons come later.

خُذْ is an exception. From أَخَذَ، يَأْخُذُ the rule would produce a form awkward on the tongue, so Arabic discarded it and kept the short خُذْ. The teacher's general point: every rule has its exceptions, and Arabic prioritises ease of pronunciation.

هَمْزَة الْوَصْل is pronounced when the word begins the utterance but dropped when something precedes it — hence مَا اسْمُكَ is read mā-smuka, and وَاذْهَبْ or فَاذْهَبْ loses the hamza sound because of the preceding letter. The rule about the hamza's vowel therefore matters only when the word comes first.
A مَفْعُول بِهِ takes a fatḥa, which is why it is اُكْتُبِ اسْمَكَ — the name is what the writing is done to.
تَحْتَ functions as a مُضَاف and a مُضَاف إِلَيْهِ at once, so it carries no tanwīn: تَحْتَ مَكْتَبِ هِشَامٍ.
نَظَرَ، يَنْظُرُ means to look, and it occurs throughout the Qur'ān, including where Mūsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام is told he will not see his Lord but should look at the mountain.

Vocabulary: عَقْرَب (scorpion, a feminine noun), حِذَاء (shoe), غُرْفَة (room), مُظْلِمَة (dark) from ظُلْمَة with its plural ظُلُمَات, جَوّ (weather, also طَقْس), حَمَّام (bathroom), دَفْتَر (notebook), and طَرَحَ (to throw).
اِقْرَأْ carries particular weight as the first word revealed of the Qur'ān.
questions: [00:17:00] Q: Is عَقْرَب feminine? — A: Yes, and the sentences about it in the lesson treat it accordingly.
[00:18:00] Q: What does تَحْتَ do to the word after it? — A: It is مُضَاف to it, so it takes no tanwīn itself — تَحْتَ مَكْتَبِ هِشَامٍ, under Hishām's desk.
[00:19:00] Q: Does اُنْظُرْ mean I think? — A: No. نَظَرَ، يَنْظُرُ means to look, so اُنْظُرْ is look.
[00:20:02] Q: Where does the plural اُقْتُلُوا occur in the Qur'ān? — A: In Sūrat Yūsuf, where the brothers say it to one another, addressing a group rather than one person.
[00:28:00] Q: Can the hamza of the command carry a fatḥa? — A: Never. It is either a ḍamma or a kasra, decided by the vowel on the third letter.

[00:32:01] Q: Why do we say مَسْمُكَ rather than مَا اسْمُكَ, and اِفْعَلُوا after a فَـ loses its hamza? — A: هَمْزَة الْوَصْل is only pronounced at the start; when a letter precedes it, it is not read.

[00:43:00] Q: Was the command given to the Prophet ﷺ about shaking the tree one of these forms? — A: That is a different pattern — from هَزَّ، يَهُزُّ one could say اُهْزُزْ by this rule, but the contracted هُزَّ, or هُزِّي for a female, is also used.

[00:43:00] Q: Do these command forms cover male, female and plural alike? — A: No, what has been learned here is the singular masculine; the others are coming, apart from the plural اُقْتُلُوا already seen.

quiz.q: How does فِعْل الْأَمْر differ in function from the مَاضِي and the مُضَارِع?
options: It is only used in questions
It asks for an action rather than giving information
quiz.a: The teacher's framing: the first two tell you something happened or is happening, while the command seeks something to happen.

quiz.q: Which form do you start from when building a command?
quiz.a: Step one is to look at the مُضَارِع, and particularly the vowel on its third letter; the past tense can be set aside.

quiz.q: What replaces the prefix letter of the مُضَارِع?
quiz.a: Step two removes the prefix and puts هَمْزَة الْوَصْل in its place.

quiz.q: What happens to the last letter?
options: It is made مَجْزُوم, that is sākin
quiz.a: اُكْتُبْ ends in a sukūn, not the ḍamma the مُضَارِع had.

quiz.q: The مُضَارِع يَكْتُبُ has a ḍamma on its third letter. What is the command?
quiz.a: A ḍamma on the third letter gives a ḍamma on the hamza: اُكْتُبْ.

quiz.q: And يَجْلِسُ, with a kasra on its third letter?
quiz.a: A kasra or a fatḥa on the third letter gives a kasra on the hamza: اِجْلِسْ.

quiz.q: Which vowel can the hamza of فِعْل الْأَمْر never take?
quiz.a: The teacher had the class cancel out fatḥa first: it is always either a ḍamma or a kasra.

quiz.q: Why is the command of أَخَذَ simply خُذْ?
options: Because it is a doubled verb
Because the regular form would be awkward to pronounce, so it was shortened
quiz.a: An exception: the expected form was clumsy on the tongue, and Arabic prefers ease of pronunciation, so خُذْ is used.

quiz.q: How is the command made plural for a group of males?
quiz.a: اُقْتُلْ addresses one person, اُقْتُلُوا a group — as in the words of Yūsuf's brothers.

quiz.q: Why is the hamza not pronounced in مَا اسْمُكَ?
options: Because هَمْزَة الْوَصْل is only pronounced when the word begins the utterance
quiz.a: With a preceding word the هَمْزَة الْوَصْل is dropped in pronunciation, so it is read mā-smuka.

quran_examples.translation: Go to Pharaoh. Indeed, he has transgressed.
quran_examples.note: The teacher's first Qur'ānic command: اِذْهَبْ from يَذْهَبُ, whose fatḥa on the third letter gives the hamza a kasra.

quran_examples.translation: Recite in the name of your Lord who created.
quran_examples.note: Noted in class as the first word revealed of the Qur'ān, and a command built from يَقْرَأُ.

quran_examples.translation: Kill Yūsuf or cast him out to another land.
quran_examples.note: The plural command the class was asked to locate, showing the wāw added for a group — and اطْرَحُوهُ beside it, from طَرَحَ, the other verb covered.

quran_examples.arabic: انظُرُوا إِلَىٰ ثَمَرِهِ إِذَا أَثْمَرَ وَيَنْعِهِ
quran_examples.transliteration: unẓurū ilā thamarihi idhā athmara wa-yanʿih
quran_examples.translation: Look at its fruit when it yields and ripens.
quran_examples.note: A student's example for اُنْظُرْ, here in the plural; يَنْظُرُ has a ḍamma on its third letter, hence the ḍamma on the hamza.

quran_examples.translation: And repel evil by that which is better.
quran_examples.note: The verb the teacher walked through step by step: يَدْفَعُ has a fatḥa on its third letter, so the command is اِدْفَعْ with a kasra — and the hamza is unpronounced here because of the preceding wāw.

quran_examples.arabic: خُذْهَا وَلَا تَخَفْ ۖ سَنُعِيدُهَا سِيرَتَهَا الْأُولَىٰ
quran_examples.transliteration: khudhhā wa-lā takhaf, sa-nuʿīduhā sīratahā al-ūlā
quran_examples.translation: Take it and fear not; We will return it to its former state.
quran_examples.note: One of several places the irregular خُذْ appears, spoken to Mūsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام about his staff.

quran_examples.arabic: خُذْ مِنْ أَمْوَالِهِمْ صَدَقَةً تُطَهِّرُهُمْ وَتُزَكِّيهِم بِهَا
quran_examples.transliteration: khudh min amwālihim ṣadaqatan tuṭahhiruhum wa-tuzakkīhim bihā
quran_examples.translation: Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them increase.
quran_examples.note: Cited among the Qur'ānic uses of خُذْ, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ.

quran_examples.translation: O Yaḥyā, take the Scripture with determination.
quran_examples.note: A third instance of خُذْ, spoken to Yaḥyā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام, with الْكِتَابَ as its مَفْعُول بِهِ carrying the fatḥa.

quran_examples.arabic: يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ
quran_examples.transliteration: yā ayyuhā al-nāsu uʿbudū rabbakumu alladhī khalaqakum
quran_examples.translation: O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you.
quran_examples.note: Raised at the end of the lesson for اُعْبُدُوا from عَبَدَ، يَعْبُدُ — the plural command, and an instance where a preceding word changes how the hamza is read.
Another example of اُنْظُرْ offered in class, here in the singular.
